cards.front: Who yields when vehicles arrive together, and when turning left?
cards.back: When vehicles reach an intersection at the same time you yield to the car on the right, and when turning left you yield to all oncoming traffic close enough to be a hazard.

cards.front: Who yields on protected routes and when entering from a driveway?
cards.back: You yield to all traffic on the protected route, stopping first where a stop is required, and you must stop and yield when entering any public street or road from an alley, driveway or farmyard.

cards.front: Who do you yield to when the light turns green?
cards.back: When a light turns green you yield to pedestrians and to vehicles still caught in the intersection before you proceed.

cards.front: Who has the right of way at intersections, and what must you not drive through?
cards.back: Funeral processions and convoys have the right of way at intersections, their vehicles usually show headlamps and the first and last vehicles carry distinctive markings, and you must not drive between the vehicles of a funeral procession.

cards.front: How does a simultaneous arrival differ from a left turn for yielding?
cards.back: At a simultaneous arrival the driver on the left yields to the car on the right, while a left-turning driver yields to oncoming traffic regardless of who arrived first.
cards.memory_hook: Right wins together, left always yields

cards.front: How does entering from a driveway differ from entering a protected route?
cards.back: Entering from an alley, driveway or farmyard requires a full stop and yield, while entering a protected route from a side road requires yielding to the protected traffic.

cards.front: How does a funeral procession's right of way differ from an emergency vehicle's?
cards.back: Funeral processions and convoys hold the right of way at intersections, while emergency vehicles take the right of way everywhere by requiring you to clear a path and stop.

cards.front: Where must you never pass on the shoulder, hill or curve?
cards.back: You must not pass on the right shoulder of the highway, and you must not pass when approaching a hill or curve without seven hundred to one thousand feet of clear distance ahead.
cards.memory_hook: No shoulder, need seven hundred feet

cards.front: When is passing unsafe because of oncoming traffic, and what is banned when passed?
cards.back: You must not pass when the maneuver cannot be completed without interfering with the safety of an oncoming vehicle and before a yellow line appears in your lane, and when you are being passed it is unlawful to increase your speed.
cards.memory_hook: Finish before yellow, never speed up

cards.front: What do a solid yellow line and a flashing school bus mean for passing?
cards.back: You must not pass when a solid yellow line is in your lane, which is announced by a yellow no passing zone pennant on the left side of the road ahead, nor when a school bus on the same roadway has its flashing lights operating.
cards.memory_hook: Solid yellow, flashing bus, no pass

cards.front: Where near intersections, crossings and bridges is passing banned?
cards.back: You must not pass within one hundred feet of or while crossing any intersection or railroad crossing, nor within one hundred feet of a posted narrow bridge, viaduct or tunnel, and the end of a no passing zone only means visibility has improved, not that passing is safe.
cards.memory_hook: Hundred feet, zone end not safe

cards.front: When is the left half of the roadway forbidden?
cards.back: The left half of the roadway is forbidden on a road with four or more lanes of moving traffic unless signs say otherwise, near the top of a hill or on a curve, within one hundred feet of or inside an intersection or railroad crossing, and within one hundred feet of a bridge or tunnel when oncoming vehicles cannot be seen.
cards.memory_hook: Four lanes, hills, curves, hundred feet

cards.front: How do the passing distances near intersections differ from hills?
cards.back: Passing is banned within one hundred feet of an intersection, railroad crossing, narrow bridge, viaduct or tunnel, while a hill or curve requires seven hundred to one thousand feet of clear distance before passing.
cards.memory_hook: Hundred near crossings, seven hundred hills

cards.front: When and how far ahead must you signal?
cards.back: You must signal every time you slow down, turn or change lanes, even when no other vehicle is in sight, and signals must be given for at least one hundred feet, about five car lengths, before the maneuver, with a longer signal advisable at higher speeds.
cards.memory_hook: Always, one hundred feet, five cars

cards.front: When must you use hand signals, and what does signaling not give you?
cards.back: Hand signals must be used when the vehicle's turn signals are not working, and signaling never gives you the right to make the move until you have checked that it can be completed without interfering with other traffic.
cards.memory_hook: Hand signals when broken, check first

cards.front: Why should you keep your foot off the brake pedal when not braking?
cards.back: Keep your foot off the brake pedal whenever you are not actually braking, because a lit stop lamp sends following drivers a false stop signal.

cards.front: When must you stop at a railroad crossing, and how far from the rail?
cards.back: You must stop at least fifteen feet from the nearest rail of a railroad crossing when an electric or mechanical signal warns of a train, when a gate is lowered or a flagman signals, when a train within one thousand five hundred feet sounds an audible warning, or when an approaching train is visible and close enough to be a hazard.

cards.front: How does the signal distance differ from the railroad stop distance?
cards.back: A turn or lane-change signal must begin at least one hundred feet ahead, while a railroad stop must be at least fifteen feet from the nearest rail.
cards.memory_hook: Hundred to signal, fifteen to rail

cards.front: How do hand signals differ from resting your foot on the brake?
cards.back: Hand signals replace turn signals only when the vehicle's signals are not working, while resting a foot on the brake pedal creates a false stop signal and must be avoided.
cards.memory_hook: Hands when broken, foot off pedal

cards.front: What is the basic speed law, and what is the major cause of crashes?
cards.back: Excessive speed for conditions is the major cause of most crashes, and the basic speed law forbids driving faster than is reasonable and prudent for the area, the road and traffic, pedestrians, weather and light.

cards.front: What speed limit rules apply, including driving too slowly?
cards.back: You must not exceed the posted maximum speed limit, must not drive below a posted minimum speed limit, and must not drive so slowly that you hold back other traffic, pulling off the road or changing route if you cannot keep up.
cards.memory_hook: No faster, no slower, no blocking

cards.front: Where should slow drivers travel on a multilane road, and what is banned?
cards.back: If you drive more slowly than traffic on a multilane road, stay in the right-hand lane so others can pass on your left, and never take part in any race, speed contest or speed exhibition on a public street or highway.

cards.front: Where do reduced speed limits apply?
cards.back: Lower speed limits apply near schools and playgrounds, at school crossing signs while children are present, and on residential and business streets.

cards.front: How does a posted minimum differ from the holding-back rule?
cards.back: Driving below a posted minimum limit is a violation, while driving so slowly that you hold back traffic is a violation even where no minimum is posted.

cards.front: What must you do when an emergency vehicle approaches with siren or flashing lights?
cards.back: When you hear an emergency vehicle's siren, bell or horn or see its flashing red or blue lamps you must give it a clear path and stop, without panicking or jamming on the brakes, by reducing speed, locating the vehicle and its direction, and moving out of its path.

cards.front: What do you do when an emergency vehicle is right behind you, or stopped ahead?
cards.back: When an emergency vehicle is right behind you in heavy traffic, continue slowly until you can clear its way, and when you come upon a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights, slow or stop as the situation demands and, if it is safe, keep an empty lane between your vehicle and it.
cards.memory_hook: Keep moving slowly, leave a lane

cards.front: What must you do before leaving a vehicle unattended?
cards.back: Before leaving a vehicle unattended, shut off the engine, lock the ignition and take the key, set the parking brake, and turn the wheels toward the curb if the vehicle is on a grade.
cards.memory_hook: Engine off, key out, brake, wheels

cards.front: How many persons in the front seat may constitute interference with the driver?
cards.back: Driving with more than three persons in the front seat may constitute interference with the driver, which is prohibited.

cards.front: How does an approaching emergency vehicle differ from a stopped one?
cards.back: For an approaching emergency vehicle you pull out of its path and stop, while for a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights you slow or stop and leave an empty lane beside it when safe.

cards.front: Where is parking prohibited because of hazards, sidewalks, driveways or intersections?
cards.back: Parking is prohibited anywhere your vehicle is hazardous to other traffic, where it will be towed, on a sidewalk, in front of or so close to a driveway that it interferes with its use, and within or so close to an intersection that it interferes with traffic.

cards.front: Where is parking prohibited near hydrants, crosswalks, signs, bridges and tunnels?
cards.back: Parking is also prohibited in front of or so close to a fire hydrant that it could interfere with the hydrant's use, on or so close to a crosswalk that it blocks drivers' view of pedestrians, where official signs or markings prohibit standing or parking, and on a bridge, elevated structure or inside a tunnel.

cards.front: What is double parking, and how far from the curb may you park?
cards.back: Double parking, stopping on the roadway side of another car at the edge of the road, is prohibited whether or not you stay in the vehicle, and so is parking more than twelve inches from the curb.

cards.front: What parking rules cover loading zones, street width and roadside repairs?
cards.back: You may not park in a passenger or freight loading zone, anywhere that leaves less than ten feet of street width for free movement of traffic, or on a public road to repair a vehicle except in an emergency, wash it, or display it for sale.
cards.memory_hook: Loading zones, ten feet, no repairs

cards.front: What rules apply to marked parking spaces and long-term parking?
cards.back: A vehicle may not be parked so that it sticks out of a marked space unless it is larger than the space, and no vehicle may stay parked on a public street or highway continuously for more than twenty-four hours.

cards.front: Who may use an accessible parking space, and what must stay clear?
cards.back: A space marked with the international symbol of accessibility may be used only when you display the placard or plate issued to the disabled person being transported, and the access aisle beside such a space must stay clear for wheelchair lifts, ramps and other mobility devices.

cards.front: What are the rules in a tow-away zone?
cards.back: In a tow-away zone you must not park or stop even momentarily during the hours on the official sign, except when blocked by traffic, and a vehicle left there is towed by the police, whom you contact for recovery information.

cards.front: How does the curb distance differ from the street width rule?
cards.back: Parking must be within twelve inches of the curb, while a street must keep at least ten feet of width free for traffic beside a parked vehicle.
cards.memory_hook: Twelve inches curb, ten feet free

cards.front: How does the twenty-four hour limit differ from a tow-away zone?
cards.back: A vehicle may stay parked on a public street for up to twenty-four hours continuously, while in a tow-away zone even a momentary stop during the posted hours is prohibited.
cards.memory_hook: Street one day, tow zone never

decks.module: Keeping right, passing right, lanes and following

cards.front: What must you obey while driving on a street or highway?
cards.back: You must obey every traffic law while driving on a street or highway, obey all lawful orders and directions of a police officer, and operate your vehicle as traffic signs, signals and pavement markings indicate.

cards.front: Which half of the roadway must you normally use, and where do slower drivers belong?
cards.back: Keep to the right half of the roadway; opposite-direction vehicles pass each other on the right, a narrow road requires leaving oncoming vehicles at least half of its main traveled portion, and a driver moving slower than other traffic belongs in the extreme right lane.
cards.memory_hook: Right half, slow in right lane

cards.front: When may you drive on the left half of the roadway?
cards.back: You may use the left half of the roadway when overtaking a vehicle going your way on a road with two or three lanes of moving traffic and no oncoming traffic, when an obstruction blocks your side and oncoming vehicles are not using the left half, or when driving on a one-way street.

cards.front: When may you pass another vehicle on the right?
cards.back: You may pass on the right of a vehicle that is about to turn left, but never by leaving the pavement or main traveled portion, and you may also pass on the right on a paved road with two or more marked lanes in your direction or on a one-way street with two or more marked lanes.

cards.front: Which direction must you drive on a one-way roadway?
cards.back: On a one-way roadway you must drive only in the direction the posted signs indicate.

cards.front: What are the rules for driving on a road marked with traffic lanes?
cards.back: On a road marked with traffic lanes you must drive entirely within one lane, change lanes only after checking that the change is safe, and use the lane the signs or pavement markings assign.
cards.memory_hook: Stay in lane, check before changing

cards.front: What following distance is required, and what extra rule applies when towing?
cards.back: Your following distance must stay reasonable and prudent for the speed, the traffic, the road and the weather, and a vehicle that is towing another must leave enough room ahead for an overtaking vehicle to move into safely.

cards.front: How does left-half use differ on two-lane versus four-lane roads?
cards.back: You may use the left half of a two or three lane road to pass when no traffic is coming, while on a road with four or more lanes the left half is off limits unless signs direct otherwise.
cards.memory_hook: Two lanes pass, four lanes no

cards.front: How does passing on the right differ from passing on the shoulder?
cards.back: Passing on the right is allowed when the vehicle ahead is turning left or when two or more lanes run your way, while passing on the right shoulder is never allowed.

cards.front: What is the slow-moving vehicle emblem, and what should you do when you see it?
cards.back: A highly reflective eighteen-inch triangular slow-moving vehicle emblem must be displayed on the rear of vehicles designed to travel at twenty-five miles per hour or less, and when you see it you should reduce speed and approach cautiously.

cards.front: How does the slow-moving emblem differ from the no passing pennant?
cards.back: The slow-moving vehicle emblem is an eighteen-inch reflective triangle for vehicles built for twenty-five miles per hour or less, while the no passing zone pennant is a yellow sign on the left side of the road.
